questions.question: What does an MQ (multivariate quadratic) public key usually look like?
options: A list of quadratic polynomials over a finite field
A single large prime modulus and a generator
A pair of elliptic-curve points
A symmetric-key and a nonce
questions.explanation: MQ signature public keys are typically presented as many quadratic equations (polynomials) in many variables over a finite field.

questions.question: In Oil-and-Vinegar trapdoors, why does fixing vinegar variables help?
options: It turns the remaining equations into a linear system in the oil variables
It makes the field prime so inverses exist
It hashes the message into a shorter digest
It compresses the public key into fewer bytes
questions.explanation: OV polynomials are constructed to avoid oil×oil terms, so once vinegars are fixed the system becomes linear in the oils.

questions.question: In this lesson's toy scheme, what condition makes `LayeredOVCentralMap._solve_layer(...)` valid?
options: The layer's polynomials contain no quadratic oil×oil terms
The signer uses SHA-256 to hash the message
The public key polynomials are dense
The modulus p is larger than the number of variables
questions.explanation: The solver probes oil variables one-at-a-time; this only works as a linear extraction if there are no oil×oil quadratic terms.

questions.question: What is the public verification equation for MQ signatures in this lesson?
options: P(signature) == H(message)
F(signature) == H(message)
S(message) == T(signature)
H(signature) == P(message)
questions.explanation: Verification evaluates the public quadratic map P on the signature and compares it to the hash digest of the message.

questions.question: Why does composing the central map with affine maps hide the Oil-and-Vinegar structure?
options: It mixes variables and outputs so the public polynomials look dense and unstructured
It removes all quadratic terms from the polynomials
It makes signing possible without solving any equations
It guarantees the public key is small
questions.explanation: Affine input/output mixing spreads structure across variables and equations, making the public system look closer to a random MQ system.

questions.question: In layered OV (Rainbow-style), what changes between Layer 1 and Layer 2 during signing?
options: Layer 2 treats all Layer-1 variables as vinegar variables and solves for new oils
Layer 2 switches from finite fields to integers
Layer 2 removes the hash function
Layer 2 replaces quadratic polynomials with elliptic curves
questions.explanation: Later layers consider previous variables as known (vinegars) and introduce additional oil variables that are solved from a new linear system.

questions.question: Why is Rainbow described as 'dead' in modern cryptography discussions?
options: Practical key-recovery attacks were found against proposed parameter sets
It requires quantum computers to verify signatures
It cannot be implemented over finite fields
It only works for one-time signatures
questions.explanation: Rainbow suffered practical cryptanalytic breaks (key recovery), so it is not considered safe to deploy.

questions.question: Which implementation issue is especially dangerous for MQ/OV signers?
options: Side-channel leakage during signing (timing/power/faults) revealing structure
Using too many print statements in verification
Storing the public key as JSON instead of bytes
Using a slow hash function like SHA-256
questions.explanation: Signing involves secret structure and linear algebra; side-channels can leak information about the trapdoor even if the math is correct.
